claim: Julie Cole's Galápagos coral study of El Niño shows that every 30-year climate normal now systematically underestimates tail events, so maintenance thresholds built on those normals will misfire.
source_title: El Niño is now stronger than at any point in the last 1,000 years, study finds
passage:
Temperature variability since 1984 runs 36.5 percent higher than it was during the preindustrial stretch from 1000 to 1850 CE and is still 16.2 percent higher than during the period from 1851 to 1982. All three intervals are statistically distinct, and the trend only goes up. Those figures, Cole explained, mean that events that once ran a degree or two above normal in the Galápagos now run three or four.

The corals also record a shift in skewness—whether the swings were lopsided in the warm or cold direction. “The skewness turned positive,” Cole said, “and the positive skewness indicates that it’s the warmer events that got stronger.”
notes: Uses the correction's quoted phrases ("systematically underestimates tail events", "will misfire"); the article covers ENSO variability only and says nothing about 30-year normals or risk models.

claim: World Labs gives the example of an Atlas reconstruction of a substation that is 80% measured and 20% imagined.
source_title: Atlas: A World Model for Spatial Intelligence
passage:
Atlas can take a variable number of input views of a scene. When parts of the world are not visible in the input views, Atlas imagines a plausible way to fill in the gaps by drawing from its rich world knowledge.

But sometimes you do not want imagination; you might want an exact reconstruction of a real-world location. Passing more input images gives Atlas more context: the more it sees, the less it imagines. Atlas typically gives faithful reconstructions with as few as two or three images, outperforming state-of-the-art results by models specially trained only for 3D reconstruction.
notes: The "80% measured, 20% imagined" phrase is quoted in the correction, but the sentence attributing it to World Labs is reconstructed; the post has no substation example.

claim: Publishing a dataset as a single PMTiles archive on S3-style object storage gives a low-cost, zero-maintenance public map that can be kept up to date with no tile server.
source_title: PMTiles Concepts (Protomaps documentation)
passage: PMTiles is a single-file archive format for pyramids of tiled data. A PMTiles archive can be hosted on a storage platform like S3, and enables low-cost, zero-maintenance map applications. Concepts ​ -   PMTiles is a general format for tiled data addressed by Z/X/Y coordinates. This can be cartographic basemap vector tiles, remote sensing observations, JPEG images, or more. -   PMTiles readers use HTTP Range Requests to fetch only the relevant tile or metadata inside a PMTiles archive on-demand. -   The arrangement of tiles and directories is designed to minimize the amount of overhead requests when panning and zooming. -   PMTiles is a read-only format. It is not possible to update an archive in-place without re-writing the entire file, similar to CSV, JSON and Parquet. If you need transactional updates, use a database like SQLite or PostgreSQL + ST_asMVT.
notes: Reconstructed from the correction; the source's 'zero-maintenance' wording supports most of it, but updates require rewriting the whole file.

claim: SpyCloud's research found that about 167 US utilities were breached through one infected device at an advanced-metering vendor.

A single compromised endpoint handed criminals identity intelligence tied to more than a hundred otherwise unrelated organizations.

claim: TerraWatch Space argues that whichever Earth observation embedding becomes the default for a region becomes the standard everyone must map into, and advises treating embeddings like a coordinate reference system.

What makes embeddings interesting is that they have now created a new potential abstraction layer in EO. Embeddings are products in their own right, rather than simply an intermediate output inside an AI pipeline.
It also creates an important dependency: embeddings are not neutral representations of the Earth. What they contain depends on the model that produced them, the data it was trained on and the patterns it was designed to preserve. In practice, this means embeddings produced by two different EOFMs likely cannot be compared or combined, unless by design.

claim: Microsoft Research has built a system that forecasts geomagnetic risk for each of 66,935 US substations 30 to 60 minutes ahead, giving utilities location-specific warning of space-weather impacts.

passage: During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid.  It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact.
notes: Omission error: the notes presented it as a Microsoft Research system without saying it was a summer intern project and research demo needing validation before operational use (stated in the source's conclusion).

claim: The Microsoft Research space-weather risk model built its substation and grid layer from HIFLD public infrastructure data.
source_title: Forecasting space weather risks on power grids
passage: The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment.  A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data.
notes: Reconstructed from the correction; the source lists GridSFM-derived grid data, not HIFLD.

claim: The Microsoft Research space-weather model detected about 80% of geomagnetic storm events over 2020 to 2026.

passage: The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest.
notes: 'About 80%' quoted from the correction; source gives 76.5%, 81.2% and 64.1% by severity.

claim: HCA's Timpani AI scheduler grants only 1% of nurses' requests for days off, according to WIRED.
source_title: AI Is Making a Mess of Nurses' Schedules. They Say It's a Safety Issue
passage: On average, Timpani schedules nurses for 1 percent of their requested days off, or what are known as red days, according to HCA. Lee Barker, an HCA nurse in Missouri, says while that number might appear relatively low, getting scheduled on red days was previously unheard of at their facility.
notes: Reconstructed from the correction; HCA says nurses are scheduled on 1 percent of their requested days off, the opposite reading.

claim: During Hurricane Ida, FloodNet sensors alerted New York City emergency management to flooding in Gowanus 50 minutes early.
source_title: Alerting Communities to Hyperlocalized Urban Flooding
passage:
The researchers created a public-facing data dashboard that allows community members and city agency personnel to visualize the data in close to real time and to access historical data. Alerts can be triggered to warn community members and emergency responders when floods are detected.
To date, the team has deployed 87 FloodNet sensors across all five boroughs of New York City, which recorded 360 flood events between October 2020 and May 2023. The team is now fine-tuning data analysis tools and flood detection thresholds and expanding the sensor network. They noted that their aim is to release flood data to stakeholders in real time, with the goal of making that data meaningful for actionable use . ( Water Resources Research , https://doi.org/10.1029/2023WR036806 , 2024)
notes: Correction says the claim was in none of the sources read (Eos and the WRR paper, which is blocked by Wiley today); Eos used as the cited source and its passage on alerts chosen; arguably 'no single source'.

claim: Mark Bauer's FloodNet NYC tutorial README sets out lessons for analysing the data, such as grouping flood events into 6-hour storm episodes and separating tidal from rain-driven flooding.
source_title: FloodNet NYC Tutorials (README)
not_replayable_reason: other: source changed since the check; the README was a stub on 2026-10-08 but now describes notebooks 05/06 covering tidal separation and the 6-hour grouping
notes: Today's README would likely support the claim, so replaying against the current source would mislabel it.

claim: Nebraska is one of the few states mandating that data centers report their water and power use, and Google's Nebraska LLCs such as Agate LLC follow a shell-unmasking pattern, according to KOLN.
source_title: Improper redaction reveals Lincoln’s Google Data Center water and electricity usage
passage:
The Department of Water, Energy, and Environment Data Center Task Force is overseeing the execution of Governor Jim Pillen’s July 20 th Executive Order requiring data centers in the state to self-report their impact on Nebraska’s resources; primarily water, power grids and local infrastructure.
Usage reports are due by Sept. 30. Submitted reports can be read here , simply enter “DCR” into the “DEQ Program” field.
notes: Combines the two quoted phrases from the correction ('one of the few states mandating this', 'shell-unmasking pattern'); KOLN only describes Nebraska's executive order and reports, with no comparison to other states.

claim: NSF's Ocean Observatories Initiative, launched in 2015, is a $368 million network of moorings, autonomous vehicles and a cabled observatory, according to Science.
source_title: Dismantling of key ocean ‘telescope’ raises fears of U.S. retreat from marine science
passage: Decades ago, watching astronomers build ever more ambitious telescopes with support from the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), oceanographers began to dream big. They wanted a comparable facility, one that could provide a continuous view of the ocean and help offset a drop in Navy research funding after the Cold War. In 2015, they got it: the Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI), a $386 million network of instrumented moorings, underwater autonomous vehicles, and a fixed, cabled observatory that would operate around the clock.
notes: $368 million is quoted from the correction; Science says $386 million. Passage fetched via Exa (site returns 403 to curl).

claim: The gaps in ocean data left by NSF pulling its Ocean Observatories Initiative moorings are a market signal for premium data products to fill them.
source_title: Northwest’s yanked ocean observatories start to return to sea
passage:
The removal of the equipment for a year or more leaves a permanent gap in the long-term data collected by the instruments.
”The toughest thing about this is to have that gap in the data,” Dever said. “Once it’s out, it’s out, and we’ll never know what the story was in between there.”
notes: Built around the quoted phrases 'market signal' and 'premium data products'; this was speculation with no source, so OPB's passage on the data gap was chosen as where it would have to be supported. Science could equally be the source.

claim: The Data Rescue Project's HIFLD Open archive can be downloaded in full as a 170 GB bulk torrent.
source_title: Federal GIS Data Saved and Archived
passage: A search for HIFLD Open in DataLumos will yield all of the records, which can be downloaded individually. The titles of the datasets and their descriptions were carried over from the old repository. Users who wish to download the entire set can follow the instructions for connecting to the Brown University Library's Globus endpoint. Globus is a mechanism for transferring big datasets; once you have a Globus account and have installed a small software package, you can search for the collection and transfer everything from a single folder.
notes: '170 GB bulk torrent' quoted from the correction; source describes a Brown University Library Globus endpoint with no size given.
